top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) credits one coherent, jointly authored body of design-based evidence: technology and import competition reshape labour demand, and local adjustment is slow, uneven and persistent. The central papers are over a decade old and have been replicated in other countries and datasets, so the live debate is about magnitude and persistence, not whether the effect exists. Attribution is clear for the import-shock papers, and Autor carries the task and technology strand. A narrow citation avoids claiming the whole task or skill-premium framework, whose authorship extends to Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane. It also avoids the ground closest to the 2023 prize. The costs are real: Katz and the education-versus-technology framing are left out, and the China-shock magnitudes remain contested. I still judge it the best-attributed, best-tested achievement on the slate. P004 is second because it is a more unified, mature field-creating programme, but its cross-country identification is weaker, Besley's share is less separable, and it sits near the 2024 prize. P003 is the same achievement with a broader but more composite attribution. P002 is a durable, defensible method contribution with a wide credit set. No award is last, since P001 is a prize-worthy achievement.
recusal_note: No tie to Autor, Dorn or Hanson is apparent from my profile. I hold an adjunct post at Chicago Booth, which is not an institutional tie to any candidate. I have long committee overlap with Hassler and Krusell and am an SSE colleague of Andersson, Dreber Almenberg and Friberg; these are ties to members, not candidates. My field is corporate finance, outside labour and trade. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
